This remarkable size is achieved through a protracted growth trajectory that spans much of the species' life. The larval phase begins after a brief incubation period, and the newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are quite diminutive. Shortly after chorion rupture, these lecithotrophic individuals carry residual yolk that sustains them before the onset of exogenous feeding. At the moment of eclosion, the wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0276 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0276 grams], a value derived from egg diameter data reported for congeneric species. This modest initial mass marks the beginning of a rapid growth phase that will ultimately lead to the massive adult proportions for which the species is known.

Field surveys and hatchery records consistently indicate that puberty occurs at a total length of 59 centimeters [Lp = 59 centimeters], a point at which the gonads begin active gametogenesis. This extraordinary adult body mass is achieved through decades of sustained feeding and growth in productive riverine and reservoir habitats. Large, gravid individuals are capable of producing substantial clutches during the spawning season, which typically occurs in late spring and early summer when water temperatures rise. The species is iteroparous, with mature adults returning to spawn annually under favorable conditions. The high fecundity associated with such large body size is a common trait among long-lived freshwater teleosts, allowing for the production of many offspring over a reproductive lifespan that can span several decades. This life-history strategy is well-suited to the variable environmental conditions of large river systems.

Lifespan data from mark-recapture studies and otolith annuli analysis indicate that Blue catfish can achieve a remarkable longevity. Senescence in these fish is gradual, with older individuals showing reduced growth increments but maintaining reproductive capacity well into their third or fourth decade. The ability to persist for so long under natural conditions is linked to the species' low natural mortality rate and its position as a top predator in many aquatic food webs.
